passage: I'm Rashmi. In my family, tears were for private rooms; my father would say "Be strong" and that was that. When Yash's grandmother passed away, his whole family cried openly at the funeral, hugging and wailing, and I stood stiff at the edge, thinking I ought to be doing something. Yash noticed and whispered, "You don't have to cry, my family just does it that way." I felt hot with embarrassment. Later I said, "In my house we didn't show it. It doesn't mean I felt less." He said, "I thought maybe you didn't care." We both laughed sadly. I still don't cry easily, but I hold his hand now, and he doesn't take it as coldness.

qa.q: What did Yash whisper to Rashmi at the funeral?
qa.a: That Rashmi did not have to cry, and that his family just does it that way.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling at the edge of the funeral?
qa.a: Stiff and embarrassed, and unsure what Rashmi ought to be doing.

qa.q: What helped Rashmi and Yash understand each other?
qa.a: They told each other what showing or hiding tears meant in their own families, and asked instead of assuming.

qa.q: How did Yash first read Rashmi's dry eyes?
qa.a: He thought maybe Rashmi didn't care.

grounding: Families differ on whether crying is encouraged or discouraged, so a young adult and their partner ask what tears and their absence mean to each.

passage: Note from Omkar, project supervisor. After the site accident review, Tushar's eyes filled and he turned away. Two colleagues joked, "Big man crying?" and Tushar went red and left the room. I followed after a few minutes and asked, "Would you like to talk, or just have some space?" He wanted space. Later he told me that where he grew up, crying was seen as weak for men, and his father had always said so. He said his skin flushes easily and people read it as embarrassment, but it can also be anger or heat. I asked how he felt instead of assuming. He said, "Sad, honestly. The colleague who was hurt is a friend of mine." I asked the two colleagues to leave the jokes out, and told Tushar the company counsellor is there if he wants.

qa.q: What did the two colleagues say to Tushar?
What was Tushar feeling, according to what he told Omkar?
qa.a: Sad, because the colleague who was hurt is a friend of his; his red face could mean embarrassment, anger or heat, so it could not have told Omkar that.

qa.q: What did Omkar do that helped?
qa.a: He offered a choice of talking or space, asked instead of assuming, and asked the colleagues to stop joking.

qa.q: How might Tushar's upbringing shape how he experiences tears?
qa.a: He grew up hearing that crying was weak for men, so he may feel ashamed when tears come.

grounding: Cultural and gender norms shape how tears and blushing are read, so a supervisor asks how a young man feels instead of assuming.
